A **statistical problem** consists of four things:

- (**data structure**) in this class our data always come as a data frame, so data structures differ according to how many columns they have and what the variable types are;
- (**target**) what unknown quantity are we trying to use the data to learn about?
- (**estimator**) how are we going to convert our data into a *best guess* (aka estimate) of the unknown target?
- (**sampling distribution**) what strategy are we going to use to approximate the sampling distribution of the estimate? We've seen two options, both of which are approximations that make assumptions and work better sometimes than others:
    - simulation (histogram)
    - mathematical (smooth curve)

In general, the simulation-based approach may be more versatile across different kinds of statistical problems. 



To illustrate all of the options we have encountered, we will use different subsets of columns in the `births14` dataset in the `openintro` package:

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(openintro)

glimpse(births14)
```

## Mathematical approximation

The central limit theorem (and other results) promises that for large enough sample size (number of rows $n$), the sampling distribution of the sample proportion will be approximately:

$$
N\left(\widehat{prop},\,SE = \sqrt{\frac{\widehat{prop}(1-\widehat{prop})}{n}}\right).
$$
